title: Degrees and Radians
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: An angle represents an amount of rotation, and that rotation can be assigned a numerical measure in more than one way. Degrees describe a rotation by dividing a full revolution into 360 equal parts, while radians describe the same rotation through the relationship between arc length and radius. Understanding both systems—and being able to move between them—is essential because trigonometry uses angles in both geometric and algebraic settings.

sections.title: Degrees: Measuring a Revolution in 360 Parts

content.text: A degree is a unit of angle measure in which one degree represents one three-hundred-sixtieth of a complete revolution. Therefore, a complete revolution measures 360°, a half revolution measures 180°, and a quarter revolution measures 90°.
The number 360 comes from the way the degree system divides a full turn. It is a convenient convention rather than a fundamental feature that every angle-measurement system must use.

Angles can also be directed. Under the usual convention, counterclockwise rotation is positive and clockwise rotation is negative. This allows degree measures to describe direction as well as the amount of rotation.
One radian is the measure of a central angle whose intercepted arc has the same length as the radius of the circle.

More generally, the radian measure of a central angle is the ratio of the intercepted arc length to the radius. If an angle intercepts an arc of length s on a circle of radius r, its radian measure is s/r.

This definition does not depend on the size of the circle. If the radius becomes larger, the arc produced by the same angle becomes larger in exactly the same proportion, so the ratio of arc length to radius remains unchanged.

sections.title: Why Radians Are a Natural Angle Measure

content.text: Radians arise directly from the geometry of a circle. Instead of first dividing a revolution into an arbitrary number of equal parts, radian measure uses two quantities already present in the circle: the arc length and the radius.

Because radian measure is a ratio of two lengths, the length units cancel. Radian measure is therefore dimensionless, even though we commonly use the word "radian" to identify the angle-measurement system.

On a circle with radius 1, the radian measure of a central angle equals the length of the intercepted arc. This makes the unit circle especially useful when connecting angles to trigonometric functions.

sections.title: Why a Full Revolution Is 2π Radians

content.text: A full revolution sweeps out the entire circumference of a circle. Since the circumference is 2πr, dividing the full arc length by the radius gives (2πr)/r = 2π.
Therefore, one full revolution is 2π radians, one half revolution is π radians, and one quarter revolution is π/2 radians.
The rotation itself has not changed when we write it as 180° or π radians. These are two numerical descriptions of the same geometric rotation.
Because 360° and 2π radians describe the same full revolution, they provide the fundamental equivalence needed to convert between the two systems.
For an angle measured as D degrees and R radians, the equality D/180 = R/π follows from the fact that 180° = π radians. This proportion can be rearranged to convert in either direction.
To convert degrees to radians, multiply the degree measure by π/180. To convert radians to degrees, multiply the radian measure by 180/π.
When possible, keep radian answers in exact form involving π rather than replacing π with a decimal. For example, 60° is exactly π/3 radians, whereas a decimal approximation is only an approximation.
The most important starting points are 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 270° = 3π/2, and 360° = 2π. These correspond to quarter, half, three-quarter, and full revolutions.
Other frequently encountered angles include multiples of 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°. Their radian equivalents are especially important later when working with trigonometric functions and the unit circle.

These angles are not a random collection to memorize. They arise naturally from familiar fractions of a circle and from the geometry of special right triangles. Their radian forms can be obtained from the degree-radian relationship.

sections.title: Negative Angles and Angles Beyond One Revolution

content.text: The sign convention used for degrees also applies to radians: counterclockwise rotation is positive and clockwise rotation is negative. Thus, a clockwise quarter-turn can be represented as -π/2 radians.
Angles do not have to stop after one revolution. A rotation through more than one full turn can have a radian measure greater than 2π, just as it can have a degree measure greater than 360°.
Different signed rotations can end on the same terminal side. This idea will become important when we work systematically with angles on a circle and identify coterminal angles.
Radian measures are often written without explicitly attaching the word "radians." For example, π/3 normally means π/3 radians when the context is angle measure.
A degree measure is normally marked with the degree symbol, such as 60°. A radian measure generally appears as a number involving π, such as π/3, although decimal radian values are also possible.
The numerical value alone does not tell us the geometric angle unless we know the measurement system. For example, 90° and 90 radians represent very different rotations.

sections.title: From Angle Measure to Angles on a Circle

content.text: Once angles can be measured in degrees or radians, we can use them to describe positions around a circle. A starting direction and an amount of rotation determine where the terminal side points.

This becomes especially powerful on the unit circle, where an angle can be associated with a point on the circle. That connection will eventually allow trigonometric functions to be understood beyond right triangles.

formulas.name: Radian Measure
formulas.explanation: The radian measure θ of a central angle is the intercepted arc length s divided by the circle's radius r.

formulas.name: Full Revolution
formulas.explanation: A complete revolution has the same geometric meaning in both angle-measurement systems.

formulas.name: Degrees to Radians
formulas.explanation: Multiply a degree measure D by π/180 to obtain the equivalent radian measure R.

formulas.name: Radians to Degrees
formulas.explanation: Multiply a radian measure R by 180/π to obtain the equivalent degree measure D.

formulas.name: Degree-Radian Proportion
formulas.explanation: This proportion expresses the equivalence 180° = π radians and can be used for conversion.

formulas.name: Common Angle Equivalents
formulas.explanation: These are the quarter-turn, half-turn, three-quarter-turn, and full-turn measures in radians.

examples.question: A central angle intercepts an arc of length 8 units on a circle of radius 4 units. What is the angle's radian measure?
examples.solution: Use θ = s/r. Here s = 8 and r = 4, so θ = 8/4 = 2 radians.

examples.question: Find the radian measure of one-third of a complete revolution.
examples.solution: A full revolution is 2π radians. One-third of a full revolution is (1/3)(2π) = 2π/3 radians.

examples.question: Find the radian measure of three-fourths of a complete revolution.
examples.solution: A full revolution is 2π radians. Therefore, three-fourths is (3/4)(2π) = 3π/2 radians.

examples.question: A ray rotates clockwise through one quarter of a full revolution. Express the rotation in radians.
examples.solution: A quarter-turn is π/2 radians. Because the rotation is clockwise, its signed measure is -π/2 radians.

examples.question: On a unit circle, a central angle intercepts an arc of length 3π/4. What is the radian measure of the angle?
examples.solution: For a unit circle, r = 1. Using θ = s/r gives θ = (3π/4)/1 = 3π/4 radians.

key_ideas: Degrees and radians are two different numerical systems for measuring the same geometric quantity: rotation.
One degree is one 360th of a complete revolution.
One radian is defined by an intercepted arc whose length equals the radius.
Radian measure is the ratio of arc length to radius: θ = s/r.
Radian measure is independent of the size of the circle.
Radian measure is dimensionless because it is a ratio of two lengths.
A full revolution is 360° or 2π radians.
A half revolution is 180° or π radians.
A quarter revolution is 90° or π/2 radians.
To convert degrees to radians, multiply by π/180.
To convert radians to degrees, multiply by 180/π.
Radians connect angle measure directly to circle geometry and become especially useful on the unit circle.
Angles can be negative or greater than one full revolution in either measurement system.
misconceptions: A radian is a fixed angle that is unrelated to the circle being used.
Changing the radius changes the radian measure of a fixed angle.
Radians and degrees describe different geometric angles.
The word radians must always be written after every radian measure.
A negative angle is physically smaller than a positive angle of the same magnitude; the sign indicates direction of rotation.
Angles cannot be larger than 360° or 2π radians.
π radians and 180° are approximately equal rather than exactly equivalent.
Every angle written without a degree symbol must be an ordinary whole-number radian value.
